hints.content:
The graph of $y=2^x$ can be transformed
to get the graph of $y=3\cdot 2^{x-4}+2$. 
[[☃ explanation 1]]

Note it is important to follow order of operations when building the function, as function transformations are not always commutative.  [[☃ explanation 2]]

options.explanation:
Suppose $f(x)=2^x$ and $g(x)=3\cdot 2^{x-4}+2$.  

>$\begin{align}f(x)&=2^x\\\\
f(x-4)&=2^{x-4}\\\\
3f(x-4)&=3\cdot 2^{x-4}\\\\
3f(x-4)+2&=3\cdot 2^{x-4}+2\\\\
\end{align}$

Notice that what is on the right-hand side of the equal sign is $g(x)$.  Therefore, $g(x)=3f(x-4)+2$.  

Since function $g$ can be built from function $f$, the graph of function $g$ is a transformation of the graph of function $f$.

Consider the graph of $y=2^x$.

If we shift the graph of $y=2^x$ down $2$ units, and then reflect this across the $x$-axis, we get the following graph.

![An exponential function graph on an x y coordinate plane. Both x and y axes scale by two. The graph decreases from the interval negative infinity to infinity. It passes through (zero, one) and (two, negative two). Its asymptote is at y equals two.](web+graphie:${☣ LOCALPATH}/images/b933a4b1e376db6a8d45454cf7b59625c351c5ec)

However, if we first reflect the graph of $y=2^x$ across the $x$-axis and then shift this graph down $2$ units, we get the following graph.

![An exponential function graph on an x y coordinate plane. Both x and y axes scale by two. The graph decreases from the interval negative infinity to infinity. It passes through (zero, negative three) and (two, negative six). Its asymptote is at y equals negative two.](web+graphie:${☣ LOCALPATH}/images/6532a044950cf696d6fbc8a2ef2c2c89f37c8635)

These graphs are not the same, indicating that the order in which you perform the transformations is important!

hints.content:
Replacing $x$ with $x-4$ shifts the graph of $y=2^x$ to the right $4$ units.


[[☃ image 1]]

options.alt: An exponential function graph and its shifted graph on an x y coordinate plane. Both x and y axes scale by two. The graph increases from the interval negative infinity to infinity. It passes through (zero, one) and (one, two). Its asymptote is at y equals zero. The shifted graph increases from the interval negative infinity to infinity. It passes through (four, one) and (five, two). Its asymptote is at y equals zero.

hints.content:
Multiplying $2^{x-4}$ by $3$ stretches the graph of $y=2^{x-4}$ vertically by a factor of $3$.  

[[☃ image 1]]

Note that the graph of the function passes through $(4,1)$ *before* the stretch, and $(4, 3 )$ *after* the stretch.  This is because each $y$-coordinate is multiplied by $3$.

options.alt: An exponential function graph and its vertically stretched graph on an x y coordinate plane. Both x and y axes scale by two. The graph increases from the interval negative infinity to infinity. It passes through (four, one) and (five, two). Its asymptote is at y equals zero. The vertically stretched graph increases from the interval negative infinity to infinity. It passes through (four, three) and (five, six). Its asymptote is at y equals zero.

hints.content:
Adding $2$ to the function shifts the graph of $y=3\cdot 2^{x-4}$ up $2$ units.

[[☃ image 1]]

Since the graph of $y=3\cdot 2^{x-4}$ had a horizontal asymptote of $y=0$, the graph of $y=3\cdot 2^{x-4}+2$ has a horizontal asymptote of $y=2$.

options.alt: An exponential function graph and its shifted graph on an x y coordinate plane. Both x and y axes scale by two. The graph increases from the interval negative infinity to infinity. It passes through (four, three) and (five, six). Its asymptote is at y equals zero. The shifted graph increases from the interval negative infinity to infinity. It passes through (four, five) and (five, eight). Its asymptote is at y equals two.

hints.content:
Note that the final function passes through the point $(4,5)$.  This is one thing that distinguishes choice $B$ from choice $D$.  

We can verify this algebraically to check our work.  [[☃ explanation 2]]

options.explanation:
When $x=4$

>$\begin{align}y&=3\cdot 2^{x-4}+2\\\\
y&=3\cdot2^{4-4}+2\\\\
y&=3\cdot 2^{0}+2\\\\
y&=3\cdot 1+2\\\\
y&=5
\end{align}$

The graph of the function passes through $(4,5)$.
